title: Acute Heart Failure Exacerbation in the Community: Diuretic Titration and Admission Triggers

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with known heart failure and worsening congestion seen in primary care or an urgent clinic: assessment, oral loop diuretic titration, diuretic resistance steps, monitoring and features that call for hospital care. Checked against the Saudi Heart Association 2023 focused update (Tables 14, 21 and 22, section 4.5.4) and NICE NG106 recommendations 1.1, 1.2.2–1.2.6, 1.8 and 1.9.1. Medicine-pathway restructure on 2026-10-18: medicines regrouped into branches, steps and give-all vs choose-one options; no dose, source or clinical claim was re-checked.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 14 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.

Medicine list restructured into a branched decision pathway on 2026-10-18. Doses, routes, adjustments, monitoring, contraindications and sources are unchanged from authoring-standard-2026-10-14-v2-investigations-live.
unverifiedSections: Neither SHA 2023 nor NICE NG106 states community admission thresholds; the admission triggers here are taken from the oxygen, ventilation, blood pressure and renal thresholds the SHA 2023 uses for hospital-level care and need local clinical review.
NICE guidance on acute heart failure (CG187) and the SHA 2019 guideline were not re-opened on 14 Oct 2026.
Oral furosemide and spironolactone doses were reused from the repository's earlier heart failure topic (FDA label) and were not re-opened.
No dose is given for bumetanide, torasemide, metolazone or acetazolamide because the sources opened do not give one.
SFDA registration and hospital formulary availability were not independently verified.

Medicine pathway: branch entry criteria, preferred options and “use when” conditions were assigned from this topic's own indications and management steps. Confirm each against the cited guideline before clinical use.

pathophysiology.summary: Decompensation is a rise in cardiac filling pressure and fluid retention in a person with chronic heart failure, usually after a trigger such as ACS, arrhythmia, hypertension, infection, non-adherence or valve disease (summarised from SHA 2023 Table 21 and Table 22). Loop diuretics relieve congestive symptoms and fluid retention and are titrated up and down to the lowest dose that keeps the person euvolaemic (NG106 1.9.1). Diuretic resistance is an insufficient response to the diuretic; adherence, fluid and salt intake, dose, dosing frequency and absorption are checked first (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4). Worsening renal function, hypotension, hypoxaemia or an inadequate response to oral therapy show that outpatient treatment is not enough (SHA 2023 Tables 14 and 22).
keyMechanisms: Decompensation is a rise in cardiac filling pressure and fluid retention in a person with chronic heart failure, usually after a trigger such as ACS, arrhythmia, hypertension, infection, non-adherence or valve disease (summarised from SHA 2023 Table 21 and Table 22).
Loop diuretics relieve congestive symptoms and fluid retention and are titrated up and down to the lowest dose that keeps the person euvolaemic (NG106 1.9.1).
Diuretic resistance is an insufficient response to the diuretic; adherence, fluid and salt intake, dose, dosing frequency and absorption are checked first (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4).
Worsening renal function, hypotension, hypoxaemia or an inadequate response to oral therapy show that outpatient treatment is not enough (SHA 2023 Tables 14 and 22).

symptoms: Worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea.
Increasing ankle or abdominal swelling and rising weight.
Reduced exercise capacity or new fatigue.
Chest pain or palpitations may point to a trigger such as ACS or arrhythmia (SHA 2023 Table 21).
physicalSigns: Fluid status: raised jugular venous pressure, oedema, basal crackles, weight change compared with dry weight (NG106 1.8.1).
Cardiac rhythm, at minimum the pulse (NG106 1.8.1).
Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation (SHA 2023 Table 22).
Blood pressure and signs of poor perfusion (SHA 2023 Table 22).
redFlags: Respiratory rate above 25 breaths a minute or SpO2 below 90%: send to hospital; this is the level at which the SHA 2023 considers non-invasive ventilation and oxygen (Table 22).
Systolic pressure below 110 mmHg with evidence of poor perfusion, or frequent systolic pressure of 90 mmHg or less: send to hospital (SHA 2023 Tables 14 and 22).
Chest pain, new arrhythmia or ECG changes suggesting a precipitating ACS or arrhythmia: send to hospital (SHA 2023 Table 21).
No improvement after a short period of oral dose escalation, or a need for intravenous loop diuretic: send to hospital (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4, Table 22).
precipitants: Acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension or valve disease (SHA 2023 Table 21).
Infection or missed doses and excess salt or fluid (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4).
New drugs that cause fluid retention or worsen renal function (check the medicine list at review; NG106 1.8.1).

differentials.condition: Acute heart failure needing hospital treatment
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Respiratory distress, hypoxaemia, hypotension or a precipitating ACS; manage with the acute heart failure pathway (SHA 2023 Table 22).
NT-proBNP below 400 ng/L in an untreated person makes heart failure less likely; review alternative causes of breathlessness and swelling (NG106 1.2.5–1.2.6).
Insufficient response despite dose increase; check adherence and intake, then escalate stepwise (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4).

ruleIn.testName: Clinical assessment of functional capacity, fluid status, rhythm, cognition and nutrition
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Adult with known heart failure and worsening symptoms
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Weight above dry weight, raised venous pressure, oedema and crackles indicate fluid overload; examine the pulse for rhythm (NG106 1.8.1).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provide more detailed monitoring if the condition has deteriorated since the last review (NG106 1.8.2).
ruleIn.normalValue: Weight at dry weight, no oedema, normal venous pressure, regular pulse

references.title: NICE NG106: Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Adult with suspected new heart failure presenting with breathlessness
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Above 2,000 ng/L: specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks; 400–2,000 ng/L: within 6 weeks (NG106 1.2.3–1.2.4).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Does not distinguish ejection-fraction types; a result below 400 ng/L in an untreated person makes heart failure less likely (NG106 1.2.5).
ruleIn.normalValue: Below 400 ng/L (47 pmol/L) in an untreated person

references.title: NICE NG106: Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management

ruleIn.testName: 12-lead ECG, chest X-ray and baseline bloods including troponin
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Adult with suspected acute decompensation at presentation
ruleIn.targetCondition: Precipitating cause such as ACS or arrhythmia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Ischaemic ECG changes, raised troponin or arrhythmia point to a trigger needing hospital care (SHA 2023 Table 21).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: SHA 2023 recommends these at admission for all with suspected acute heart failure: ECG, chest X-ray, troponin, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose, blood count, liver function and TSH (Table 21).
ruleIn.normalValue: Sinus rhythm, no acute ischaemic change, troponin below the 99th percentile

references.title: 2023 National Heart Center/Saudi Heart Association focused update of the 2019 SHA guidelines for the management of heart failure
references.edition: SHA 2023 focused update, J Saudi Heart Assoc 2023;35(1), Table 21

ruleIn.testName: Iron status: ferritin, transferrin saturation and haemoglobin
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Venous blood tests in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
ruleIn.targetCondition: Iron deficiency or anaemia worsening heart failure symptoms
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Ferritin below 100 ng/mL or transferrin saturation below 20%, with haemoglobin below 150 g/L
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Consider intravenous iron in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction with these results. If iron deficiency anaemia is found, do not assume heart failure is the cause; look for other causes.
ruleIn.normalValue: Ferritin 100 ng/mL or more and transferrin saturation 20% or more; haemoglobin local adult range

references.title: NICE NG106: Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Every person with heart failure, and after each diuretic change
ruleOut.targetCondition: Worsening renal function or electrolyte disturbance
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Progressive renal deterioration or sodium below 134 mEq/L marks advanced disease or an unsafe outpatient plan (SHA 2023 Table 14).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Monitor renal function and electrolytes during diuretic use (SHA 2023 Table 22; NG106 1.8.1).
ruleOut.normalValue: Creatinine and urea in the local reference range; sodium 135–145 mmol/L; potassium 3.5–5.0 mmol/L

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Adult with a new diagnosis or a change in clinical state
ruleOut.expectedFinding: New or worse left ventricular dysfunction or valve disease needs specialist review (SHA 2023 Table 21).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Immediately when haemodynamically unstable; within 48 hours when cardiac structure and function are unknown or may have changed (SHA 2023 Table 21).
ruleOut.normalValue: Ejection fraction and valves as at the previous study

ruleOut.testName: Thyroid, liver and lipid profile, HbA1c, full blood count and urinalysis
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Venous blood tests and urine dipstick, with ECG and chest X-ray
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Abnormal thyroid, liver, glucose or blood count results, or proteinuria
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Perform an ECG and consider these tests to find aggravating factors or another diagnosis. Peak flow or spirometry also helps exclude lung disease.
ruleOut.normalValue: TSH about 0.4–4.0 mIU/L; ALT up to about 40 U/L; HbA1c below 42 mmol/mol (6.0%); urine protein negative (typical adult values; local ranges apply)

clinicalManagement.title: Triage the visit
actions: Check respiratory rate, SpO2, blood pressure, pulse and perfusion (SHA 2023 Table 22).
Send to hospital for any red flag above; do not start oral escalation first (SHA 2023 Tables 14, 21 and 22).
Otherwise assess fluid status, weight against dry weight, rhythm and medicines (NG106 1.8.1–1.8.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Tests at the visit
actions: ECG, chest X-ray and bloods including troponin, renal function, electrolytes, glucose, blood count, liver tests and TSH (SHA 2023 Table 21).
NT-proBNP if heart failure is not already confirmed; refer by band (NG106 1.2.2–1.2.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Titrate the oral loop diuretic
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Review in days to 2 weeks after each change (NG106 1.8.3); no sooner than 6–8 hours between increases
actions: Use the lowest dose that keeps the person euvolaemic, titrated up and down (NG106 1.9.1).
Increase furosemide by 20–40 mg per step, no sooner than 6–8 hours after the last dose (label, reused from the earlier topic).
Reassess weight, symptoms, blood pressure, renal function and potassium after each change; monitoring interval of days to 2 weeks after any change (NG106 1.8.3).

clinicalManagement.title: If the response is poor
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At the next review after a dose increase
actions: Check adherence and salt and fluid intake (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4).
Increase the dose, give at least twice daily or on an empty stomach, or consider switching to bumetanide or torasemide (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4).
Add or increase an MRA; a loop plus thiazide or metolazone may be used with specialist advice (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4).
Still congested, or any trigger from the red-flag list: arrange hospital care and intravenous diuretic (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4, Table 22).

clinicalManagement.title: Specialist input
actions: Recently decompensated or advanced heart failure belongs with the specialist heart failure team (NG106 1.1.2).
Share any changes with the specialist team and confirm the care plan including symptoms to watch and urgent contacts (NG106 1.1.4, 1.1.8).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitoring after stabilisation
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Days to 2 weeks, then at least 6-monthly
actions: Review function, fluid status, rhythm, medicines, renal function, iron status and haemoglobin (NG106 1.8.1).
Use a short monitoring interval after a change, at least every 6 months once stable (NG106 1.8.3).

regimens.indication: Congestion in chronic heart failure; lowest dose that keeps the person euvolaemic, titrated up and down (NICE NG106 1.9.1)
regimens.dose: 20–80 mg as a single dose; increase by 20–40 mg no sooner than 6–8 h
regimens.duration: Lowest dose that keeps euvolaemia; SHA usual 40–240 mg/day
adjustments: Increase by 20–40 mg no sooner than 6–8 hours after a dose (label)
Insufficient response: check adherence and salt and fluid intake, then raise the dose or give at least twice daily or on an empty stomach (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4)
Switching to bumetanide or torasemide may be considered (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4)

medicationPlan.note: NICE NG106 recommends diuretics at the lowest dose that relieves congestion and gives no doses (1.9.1). The furosemide and spironolactone doses and monitoring are from the repository's earlier heart failure topic (FDA label) and SHA 2023 section 4.5.4; SHA gives a usual furosemide range of 40–240 mg a day in that topic. Intravenous diuretic doses belong to the acute heart failure topic. SFDA registration was not verified. Check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: SpO2 below 90% (oxygen); respiratory rate above 25 breaths a minute with SpO2 below 90% (non-invasive ventilation) (SHA 2023 Table 22)
Systolic below 110 mmHg with hypoperfusion considered for inotropes; frequent systolic 90 mmHg or less is an advanced heart failure criterion (SHA 2023 Tables 14 and 22)
Diuretic need above furosemide equivalent 160 mg a day or supplemental metolazone; serum sodium below 134 mEq/L; progressive renal or hepatic deterioration (SHA 2023 Table 14)

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: NT-proBNP in suspected new heart failure
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Above 2,000 ng/L: specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks; 400–2,000 ng/L: within 6 weeks; below 400 ng/L makes heart failure less likely (NG106 1.2.3–1.2.5)
Days to every 2 weeks when condition or medication has changed; at least every 6 months when stable (NG106 1.8.3)

teaching.scope: Adults with known heart failure and worsening congestion seen in primary care or an urgent clinic: assessment, oral loop diuretic titration, diuretic resistance steps, monitoring and features that call for hospital care. Checked against the Saudi Heart Association 2023 focused update (Tables 14, 21 and 22, section 4.5.4) and NICE NG106 recommendations 1.1, 1.2.2–1.2.6, 1.8 and 1.9.1.
learningObjectives: Recognise features that mean hospital care rather than oral titration.
Titrate and escalate a loop diuretic safely with renal and electrolyte monitoring.
pitfalls: Escalating the diuretic in a person with hypoxaemia, hypotension or chest pain who needs hospital.
Increasing doses without checking potassium and renal function.
Forgetting adherence and salt and fluid intake before calling it resistance.
Leaving a recently decompensated person without specialist follow-up.
keyPoints: Lowest effective dose, titrated up and down (NG106 1.9.1).
Review within days to 2 weeks after any change (NG106 1.8.3).
Diuretic resistance: adherence, intake, dose and frequency first, then add an MRA or a second diuretic with specialist advice.
SpO2 below 90%, respiratory rate above 25 or systolic below 110 mmHg with poor perfusion needs hospital.

patientEducation: Weigh every morning and report a gain over the agreed limit or new breathlessness or swelling (NG106 1.8.4).
Know which symptoms need an emergency call: breathlessness at rest, chest pain, fainting (NG106 1.1.8).
lifestyleAndDiet: Follow the advised salt and fluid intake (SHA 2023 section 4.5.4).
Stay active and keep to prescribed medicines; avoid new over-the-counter drugs without checking.
mdtReferrals: Specialist heart failure team for recently decompensated or advanced heart failure (NG106 1.1.2).
Heart failure nurse as named coordinator (NG106 1.1.8).
Renal service if renal function worsens on diuretics.
dischargeCriteria: Weight stable at dry weight and symptoms improved on an oral regimen.
Renal function and potassium checked after the last dose change.
Written care plan with deterioration symptoms and contact details given (NG106 1.1.8–1.1.9).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review within days to 2 weeks after any change in diuretic or medication, then at least every 6 months with the primary care team (NG106 1.1.4, 1.8.3).
